answer:
The person described is **Martin Luther**, a German priest who sought to reform the **Catholic Church** (the religion associated with Jesus and referenced in the query as "Jesus Varela's religion," likely a conflation or typo for "Jesus' religion" or similar). Luther preached a notable sermon on **Marian devotion** (often interpreted as ironic or critical of excessive Marian intercession) in the city of **Wittenberg** shortly before his death in February 1546.

The district (or city-in-district status) of **Wittenberg** is located in the state of **Saxony-Anhalt** (in modern-day Germany). Historically, it has been associated with the Duchy/Sovereign Principality of Saxony, but since reunification, it falls under **Saxony-Anhalt**.

Answer: **Saxony-Anhalt**

**Jesus Ybiernas Varela** (December 18, 1927 – February 23, 2018) was a Filipinoprelate of the Catholic Church. He became the Bishop Emeritus of the Diocese of Sorsogon on his retirement on April 16, 2003. He was appointed bishop of Sorsogon on November 27, 1980. Prior to that he served as the first ever sitting Bishop of the Diocese of Ozamis. He also served as the Auxiliary Bishop of the Archdiocese of Zamboanga and titular Bishop of Tatilti.
| Styles of **Jesus Y. Varela** |  
| --- |  
|  |  
| Reference style | Most Reverend |  
| Spoken style | Your Excellency |  
| Religious style | Bishop |
He was born on December 18, 1927, in Bacolod, the son of Vicente Varela, a judge from Bago within the same province of Negros Occidental. He is a direct descendant of Gregorio Varela a Spaniard who was one of Bago's founding fathers, and through Gregorio's wife Josefa Araneta he is a member of the Araneta family.

Varela attended the Colegio Del Sagrado Corazon in Iloilo City for kindergarten, and the Iloilo Normal School for half of his elementary years. When his father was appointed a provincial judge in Surigao, he transferred to the Surigao Elementary School. The family later moved to Sorsogon when his father was reassigned. He studied at the Sorsogon National High School between 1946 and 1949, after which he studied for three years at the Our Lady of Peñafrancia Minor Seminary. Later, he also studied in the University of Santo Tomas in Manila, earning a Ph.L. degree in 1952. Between 1958 and 1961 he completed coursework at the University of the Angelicum in Rome.
Varela was ordained on March 17, 1956 in Cebu City, where his father last served as a Provincial Judge. He joined the Society of Jesus, following in the footsteps of his older brother Fr. Mariano Varela, who was a Jesuit priest. Later on his two younger sisters and one of his cousins became nuns. The latest in the family to join the religious service is his nephew Fr. Richard Varela of the Salesian Order.
His family is also involved in government, his nephew the late Francis Varela[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesus_Varela#cite_note-1) served as Undersecretary for Finance of the Department of Education (Philippines), and his cousin the late Jose Varela, served as Deputy Minister of Energy of Philippines and later was elected an Assemblyman for Negros Occidental.
In addition to his service as a bishop, Varela was involved in broadcasting. In 1972, he served as the Vice President of UNDA, a Catholic radio and television organization, and in 1974 he became its president. He was also President of the Philippine Federation of Catholic Broadcasters, and used this position to criticize President Ferdinand Marcos, at a time when all media were censored or under the direct control of the government.

He also served as Chairman of the Episcopal Commission on Family and Life, of the [Catholic Bishops' Conference of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Bishops'_Conference_of_the_Philippines "Catholic Bishops' Conference of the Philippines"), and was a member of its permanent council (to which all Filipino Catholic bishops belong).

Honoring Bishop Jesus Y. Varela: A Legacy of Faith and Service
Bishop Emeritus Jesus Ybiernas Varela (1927–2018) left an indelible mark on the Diocese of Sorsogon. Appointed as bishop in 1980, he shepherded the faithful for more than two decades until his retirement in 2003. His leadership was defined by deep pastoral care, a commitment to family and life, and a vision for evangelization that reached beyond the walls of the cathedral.
The Diocese of Sorsogon remembers him not only as a bishop but as a father, teacher, and servant of God. His legacy continues to inspire priests, lay leaders, and communities to live with faith, simplicity, and service.

Title: Venerable Fr. Felix Varela - Our First Pastor
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
**FOR A DISTINGUISHED NATIVE OF THE CARIBBEAN**, it was a rude welcome to America. Fr. Félix Varela, a renowned Cuban philosopher, educator, writer, and statesman, arrived in New York Harbor on December 15, 1823, disembarking from the cargo ship Draper C. Thorndike and stepping into a full-blown blizzard. Unfamiliar with the perils of walking in a northern winter, on his first steps in the country where he would live the next three decades, he slipped and fell on an icy walkway.
It was an unaccustomed low point in the life of the 35-year-old priest. A few weeks earlier, he had been representing Cuba, then a Spanish colony, as a delegate to the nascent legislative assembly at Cádiz, Spain. In a swift turn of events, the deposed Spanish king had been restored to power and ordered the execution of all who had advocated democracy. Facing certain death if he remained in Europe or returned to his beloved Cuba, Varela escaped at night to Gibraltar, where he boarded the _Thorndike,_ bound for New York.
Suddenly an exile, the thin priest in his thin cloak stood up from the icy harborside pavement and found his footing in the streets of a new city. Over the next quarter of a century, he would become a humble but prominent force in the Catholic community there, serving the faithful of New York with a selfless devotion that matched the patriotic fervor he felt for his homeland.
> **_"FATHER VARELA . . . HELPS US TO LIVE OUR FAITH AS A FORCE FOR CHANGE IN SOCIETY. SEEING HIS EXAMPLE, WE CAN OFFER OUR OWN CONTRIBUTION WITH THE SAME ENTHUSIASM THAT HE HAD FOR HELPING THE SOCIETIES OF HIS TIME TO LIVE ACCORDING TO JUSTICE AND TRUTH."_**  
> ARCHBISHOP VINCENZO PAGLIA, POSTULATOR IN VARELA’S CAUSE FOR CANONIZATION

Félix Varela would never again set foot in Cuba, but he also never stopped working on behalf of its people, pointing the way for them toward a freedom that would not come in his lifetime. Two centuries later, he is still revered by Cubans and Cuban-Americans of all political persuasions. The cause for his canonization, initiated in the 1980s, is principally overseen by the Archdiocese of Havana. But it is his life after 1823 – his years as a New York priest – that mark Varela unmistakably as a man of God.
**FÉLIX VARELA Y MORALES WAS BORN**into a military family in Havana, Cuba, in 1788. Orphaned at the age of 3, he was raised by his paternal grandparents in St. Augustine, Florida, where his grandfather was commander of the Spanish garrison. An intelligent, curious child, slight in stature, young Félix took eagerly to his studies in Latin, religion, and history.
When Varela was 14, his grandfather told him it was time to turn from academic pursuits and enroll in military training. The boy politely refused. “I want to be a soldier of Jesus Christ,” he said. When the commander became angry, Félix responded, “I don’t wish to kill men. I want to save their souls.” Though he was not destined to be a warrior, young Varela did not lack for courage.
Instead of a military academy, his grandfather sent Varela to the Seminary of San Carlos in Havana. There the young man was quickly recognized as a rising star. He became a priest, a professor, and by his mid-twenties, one of the colony’s foremost philosophers and thinkers.
As a professor and speaker, Varela showed no fear in exploring and expanding the potentially dangerous ideas of the era he lived in: the abolition of slavery, the overthrow of absolute monarchies and colonial empires. He became known as a speaker who explained ideas so clearly and persuasively that even those who disagreed with him sat up and listened. As a writer, teacher, and delegate to the Spanish Cortes, the priest stood up for what he believed in.

**AFTER HIS LANDING IN AMERICA**, it took Varela more than a year to get his credentials verified to serve as a priest in the Diocese of New York. By February 1825, he had begun serving as a parochial vicar at St. Peter’s Church on Barclay Street in Manhattan. He had learned to speak English, and had begun to settle into his duties: saying Mass, hearing confessions, performing baptisms, visiting the sick. In the evenings, the priest also found time to write and edit _El Habanero_, a magazine for Cuban readers. And the rulers of Spain and Cuba still wanted him dead.
In March 1825, an assassin landed in New York City, dispatched by associates of Francisco Vives, the colonial governor of Cuba. His instructions: to kill Fr. Félix Varela.
The priest received a letter of warning. His friends in the Cuban expatriate community were able to learn the assassin’s identity, but not his whereabouts. They entreated Varela to go into hiding, but he refused. Instead, he went about his business apparently unperturbed. He was not going to let threats turn him from his new mission of helping to build the Catholic Church in America, ministering to the needs of its people.
One day, walking the streets of his parish, the priest encountered the man who had been sent to murder him. In a spirit of compassionate forgiveness, he approached the would-be assassin and counseled him against committing a grave sin. The man listened. Then he returned to Cuba, his mission unfulfilled, while Varela carried on his own with hardly a pause.
**BEFORE THE AMERICAN REVOLUTION**, under British rule, Catholicism was banned in New York. Five decades later, as Varela began his priesthood there, a strong anti-Catholic sentiment still prevailed among many in the Protestant majority. Catholics had to be careful. They could be assaulted in the streets. On one occasion, hundreds of Catholics had to form a human shield around St. Patrick’s Cathedral on Mulberry Street (now known as the Basilica of Old St. Patrick’s Cathedral) to stop a Protestant mob from ransacking and burning it.

There were two Catholic churches in New York City in 1825: St. Patrick’s Cathedral and St. Peter’s Church on Barclay Street. The diocese opened a third, St. Mary’s, in a former Presbyterian church building on Sheriff Street, in 1826; and the following year, Varela, using his own funds and money raised from the community, purchased a fourth: an old Episcopal church in Ann Street called Christ Church. Varela became pastor of a new Catholic parish there. Its population was generally very poor, and most of the money to operate it came from Varela’s supporters in Cuba and New York.
> **_"FATHER VARELA DEDICATED HIS LIFE TO THE SICK, THE POOR, AND THE HELPLESS. HE WAS CALLED ‘THE APOSTLE OF THE IRISH’ FOR HIS WORK WELCOMING IMMIGRANTS AND TENDING TO THEIR NEEDS."_**  
> BISHOP OCTAVIO CISNEROS, VICE POSTULATOR IN VARELA’S CAUSE FOR CANONIZATION
The skills and the passion for justice that Félix Varela had developed in the first 35 years of his life turned out to be just what the Catholic Church in New York needed. His command of the principals of governing served the Church well when parish board members made unruly demands; his problem-solving skills helped keep parishes financially solvent; and his command of language enabled him to build strong community bonds. His talents at oratory captivated congregations during his homilies and, at public forums, unmasked the distortions of demagogues fomenting anti-Catholic sentiment.
Soon he was writing articles in English and co-publishing the _New York Weekly Register and Catholic Diary,_ which was widely read among the immigrant Irish. He wrote an English-language catechism for religious education and opened free Catholic schools for girls and boys next door to Christ Church, where he oversaw instruction and taught many classes himself. The schoolchildren there could hardly have imagined they were being taught by one of the most celebrated professors in the Americas.

Honoring Bishop Jesus Y. Varela: A Legacy of Faith and Service
Bishop Emeritus Jesus Ybiernas Varela (1927–2018) left an indelible mark on the Diocese of Sorsogon. Appointed as bishop in 1980, he shepherded the faithful for more than two decades until his retirement in 2003. His leadership was defined by deep pastoral care, a commitment to family and life, and a vision for evangelization that reached beyond the walls of the cathedral.
The Diocese of Sorsogon remembers him not only as a bishop but as a father, teacher, and servant of God. His legacy continues to inspire priests, lay leaders, and communities to live with faith, simplicity, and service.

**Jesus Ybiernas Varela** (December 18, 1927 – February 23, 2018) was a Filipinoprelate of the Catholic Church. He became the Bishop Emeritus of the Diocese of Sorsogon on his retirement on April 16, 2003. He was appointed bishop of Sorsogon on November 27, 1980. Prior to that he served as the first ever sitting Bishop of the Diocese of Ozamis. He also served as the Auxiliary Bishop of the Archdiocese of Zamboanga and titular Bishop of Tatilti.
| Styles of **Jesus Y. Varela** |  
| --- |  
|  |  
| Reference style | Most Reverend |  
| Spoken style | Your Excellency |  
| Religious style | Bishop |
He was born on December 18, 1927, in Bacolod, the son of Vicente Varela, a judge from Bago within the same province of Negros Occidental. He is a direct descendant of Gregorio Varela a Spaniard who was one of Bago's founding fathers, and through Gregorio's wife Josefa Araneta he is a member of the Araneta family.
texts.1:
Varela attended the Colegio Del Sagrado Corazon in Iloilo City for kindergarten, and the Iloilo Normal School for half of his elementary years. When his father was appointed a provincial judge in Surigao, he transferred to the Surigao Elementary School. The family later moved to Sorsogon when his father was reassigned. He studied at the Sorsogon National High School between 1946 and 1949, after which he studied for three years at the Our Lady of Peñafrancia Minor Seminary. Later, he also studied in the University of Santo Tomas in Manila, earning a Ph.L. degree in 1952. Between 1958 and 1961 he completed coursework at the University of the Angelicum in Rome.
Varela was ordained on March 17, 1956 in Cebu City, where his father last served as a Provincial Judge. He joined the Society of Jesus, following in the footsteps of his older brother Fr. Mariano Varela, who was a Jesuit priest. Later on his two younger sisters and one of his cousins became nuns. The latest in the family to join the religious service is his nephew Fr. Richard Varela of the Salesian Order.
His family is also involved in government, his nephew the late Francis Varela[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesus_Varela#cite_note-1) served as Undersecretary for Finance of the Department of Education (Philippines), and his cousin the late Jose Varela, served as Deputy Minister of Energy of Philippines and later was elected an Assemblyman for Negros Occidental.
In addition to his service as a bishop, Varela was involved in broadcasting. In 1972, he served as the Vice President of UNDA, a Catholic radio and television organization, and in 1974 he became its president. He was also President of the Philippine Federation of Catholic Broadcasters, and used this position to criticize President Ferdinand Marcos, at a time when all media were censored or under the direct control of the government.
texts.2:
He also served as Chairman of the Episcopal Commission on Family and Life, of the [Catholic Bishops' Conference of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Bishops'_Conference_of_the_Philippines "Catholic Bishops' Conference of the Philippines"), and was a member of its permanent council (to which all Filipino Catholic bishops belong).

**FOR A DISTINGUISHED NATIVE OF THE CARIBBEAN**, it was a rude welcome to America. Fr. Félix Varela, a renowned Cuban philosopher, educator, writer, and statesman, arrived in New York Harbor on December 15, 1823, disembarking from the cargo ship Draper C. Thorndike and stepping into a full-blown blizzard. Unfamiliar with the perils of walking in a northern winter, on his first steps in the country where he would live the next three decades, he slipped and fell on an icy walkway.
It was an unaccustomed low point in the life of the 35-year-old priest. A few weeks earlier, he had been representing Cuba, then a Spanish colony, as a delegate to the nascent legislative assembly at Cádiz, Spain. In a swift turn of events, the deposed Spanish king had been restored to power and ordered the execution of all who had advocated democracy. Facing certain death if he remained in Europe or returned to his beloved Cuba, Varela escaped at night to Gibraltar, where he boarded the _Thorndike,_ bound for New York.
Suddenly an exile, the thin priest in his thin cloak stood up from the icy harborside pavement and found his footing in the streets of a new city. Over the next quarter of a century, he would become a humble but prominent force in the Catholic community there, serving the faithful of New York with a selfless devotion that matched the patriotic fervor he felt for his homeland.
> **_"FATHER VARELA . . . HELPS US TO LIVE OUR FAITH AS A FORCE FOR CHANGE IN SOCIETY. SEEING HIS EXAMPLE, WE CAN OFFER OUR OWN CONTRIBUTION WITH THE SAME ENTHUSIASM THAT HE HAD FOR HELPING THE SOCIETIES OF HIS TIME TO LIVE ACCORDING TO JUSTICE AND TRUTH."_**  
> ARCHBISHOP VINCENZO PAGLIA, POSTULATOR IN VARELA’S CAUSE FOR CANONIZATION
texts.1:
Félix Varela would never again set foot in Cuba, but he also never stopped working on behalf of its people, pointing the way for them toward a freedom that would not come in his lifetime. Two centuries later, he is still revered by Cubans and Cuban-Americans of all political persuasions. The cause for his canonization, initiated in the 1980s, is principally overseen by the Archdiocese of Havana. But it is his life after 1823 – his years as a New York priest – that mark Varela unmistakably as a man of God.
**FÉLIX VARELA Y MORALES WAS BORN**into a military family in Havana, Cuba, in 1788. Orphaned at the age of 3, he was raised by his paternal grandparents in St. Augustine, Florida, where his grandfather was commander of the Spanish garrison. An intelligent, curious child, slight in stature, young Félix took eagerly to his studies in Latin, religion, and history.
When Varela was 14, his grandfather told him it was time to turn from academic pursuits and enroll in military training. The boy politely refused. “I want to be a soldier of Jesus Christ,” he said. When the commander became angry, Félix responded, “I don’t wish to kill men. I want to save their souls.” Though he was not destined to be a warrior, young Varela did not lack for courage.
Instead of a military academy, his grandfather sent Varela to the Seminary of San Carlos in Havana. There the young man was quickly recognized as a rising star. He became a priest, a professor, and by his mid-twenties, one of the colony’s foremost philosophers and thinkers.
As a professor and speaker, Varela showed no fear in exploring and expanding the potentially dangerous ideas of the era he lived in: the abolition of slavery, the overthrow of absolute monarchies and colonial empires. He became known as a speaker who explained ideas so clearly and persuasively that even those who disagreed with him sat up and listened. As a writer, teacher, and delegate to the Spanish Cortes, the priest stood up for what he believed in.
texts.2:
**AFTER HIS LANDING IN AMERICA**, it took Varela more than a year to get his credentials verified to serve as a priest in the Diocese of New York. By February 1825, he had begun serving as a parochial vicar at St. Peter’s Church on Barclay Street in Manhattan. He had learned to speak English, and had begun to settle into his duties: saying Mass, hearing confessions, performing baptisms, visiting the sick. In the evenings, the priest also found time to write and edit _El Habanero_, a magazine for Cuban readers. And the rulers of Spain and Cuba still wanted him dead.
In March 1825, an assassin landed in New York City, dispatched by associates of Francisco Vives, the colonial governor of Cuba. His instructions: to kill Fr. Félix Varela.
The priest received a letter of warning. His friends in the Cuban expatriate community were able to learn the assassin’s identity, but not his whereabouts. They entreated Varela to go into hiding, but he refused. Instead, he went about his business apparently unperturbed. He was not going to let threats turn him from his new mission of helping to build the Catholic Church in America, ministering to the needs of its people.
One day, walking the streets of his parish, the priest encountered the man who had been sent to murder him. In a spirit of compassionate forgiveness, he approached the would-be assassin and counseled him against committing a grave sin. The man listened. Then he returned to Cuba, his mission unfulfilled, while Varela carried on his own with hardly a pause.
**BEFORE THE AMERICAN REVOLUTION**, under British rule, Catholicism was banned in New York. Five decades later, as Varela began his priesthood there, a strong anti-Catholic sentiment still prevailed among many in the Protestant majority. Catholics had to be careful. They could be assaulted in the streets. On one occasion, hundreds of Catholics had to form a human shield around St. Patrick’s Cathedral on Mulberry Street (now known as the Basilica of Old St. Patrick’s Cathedral) to stop a Protestant mob from ransacking and burning it.
texts.3:
There were two Catholic churches in New York City in 1825: St. Patrick’s Cathedral and St. Peter’s Church on Barclay Street. The diocese opened a third, St. Mary’s, in a former Presbyterian church building on Sheriff Street, in 1826; and the following year, Varela, using his own funds and money raised from the community, purchased a fourth: an old Episcopal church in Ann Street called Christ Church. Varela became pastor of a new Catholic parish there. Its population was generally very poor, and most of the money to operate it came from Varela’s supporters in Cuba and New York.
> **_"FATHER VARELA DEDICATED HIS LIFE TO THE SICK, THE POOR, AND THE HELPLESS. HE WAS CALLED ‘THE APOSTLE OF THE IRISH’ FOR HIS WORK WELCOMING IMMIGRANTS AND TENDING TO THEIR NEEDS."_**  
> BISHOP OCTAVIO CISNEROS, VICE POSTULATOR IN VARELA’S CAUSE FOR CANONIZATION
The skills and the passion for justice that Félix Varela had developed in the first 35 years of his life turned out to be just what the Catholic Church in New York needed. His command of the principals of governing served the Church well when parish board members made unruly demands; his problem-solving skills helped keep parishes financially solvent; and his command of language enabled him to build strong community bonds. His talents at oratory captivated congregations during his homilies and, at public forums, unmasked the distortions of demagogues fomenting anti-Catholic sentiment.
Soon he was writing articles in English and co-publishing the _New York Weekly Register and Catholic Diary,_ which was widely read among the immigrant Irish. He wrote an English-language catechism for religious education and opened free Catholic schools for girls and boys next door to Christ Church, where he oversaw instruction and taught many classes himself. The schoolchildren there could hardly have imagined they were being taught by one of the most celebrated professors in the Americas.

Honoring Bishop Jesus Y. Varela: A Legacy of Faith and Service
Bishop Emeritus Jesus Ybiernas Varela (1927–2018) left an indelible mark on the Diocese of Sorsogon. Appointed as bishop in 1980, he shepherded the faithful for more than two decades until his retirement in 2003. His leadership was defined by deep pastoral care, a commitment to family and life, and a vision for evangelization that reached beyond the walls of the cathedral.
The Diocese of Sorsogon remembers him not only as a bishop but as a father, teacher, and servant of God. His legacy continues to inspire priests, lay leaders, and communities to live with faith, simplicity, and service.

**Jesus Ybiernas Varela** (December 18, 1927 – February 23, 2018) was a Filipinoprelate of the Catholic Church. He became the Bishop Emeritus of the Diocese of Sorsogon on his retirement on April 16, 2003. He was appointed bishop of Sorsogon on November 27, 1980. Prior to that he served as the first ever sitting Bishop of the Diocese of Ozamis. He also served as the Auxiliary Bishop of the Archdiocese of Zamboanga and titular Bishop of Tatilti.

He was born on December 18, 1927, in Bacolod, the son of Vicente Varela, a judge from Bago within the same province of Negros Occidental. He is a direct descendant of Gregorio Varela a Spaniard who was one of Bago's founding fathers, and through Gregorio's wife Josefa Araneta he is a member of the Araneta family.

Varela attended the Colegio Del Sagrado Corazon in Iloilo City for kindergarten, and the Iloilo Normal School for half of his elementary years. When his father was appointed a provincial judge in Surigao, he transferred to the Surigao Elementary School. The family later moved to Sorsogon when his father was reassigned. He studied at the Sorsogon National High School between 1946 and 1949, after which he studied for three years at the Our Lady of Peñafrancia Minor Seminary. Later, he also studied in the University of Santo Tomas in Manila, earning a Ph.L. degree in 1952. Between 1958 and 1961 he completed coursework at the University of the Angelicum in Rome.
Varela was ordained on March 17, 1956 in Cebu City, where his father last served as a Provincial Judge. He joined the Society of Jesus, following in the footsteps of his older brother Fr. Mariano Varela, who was a Jesuit priest. Later on his two younger sisters and one of his cousins became nuns. The latest in the family to join the religious service is his nephew Fr. Richard Varela of the Salesian Order.
His family is also involved in government, his nephew the late Francis Varela[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesus_Varela#cite_note-1) served as Undersecretary for Finance of the Department of Education (Philippines), and his cousin the late Jose Varela, served as Deputy Minister of Energy of Philippines and later was elected an Assemblyman for Negros Occidental.
In addition to his service as a bishop, Varela was involved in broadcasting. In 1972, he served as the Vice President of UNDA, a Catholic radio and television organization, and in 1974 he became its president. He was also President of the Philippine Federation of Catholic Broadcasters, and used this position to criticize President Ferdinand Marcos, at a time when all media were censored or under the direct control of the government.

He also served as Chairman of the Episcopal Commission on Family and Life, of the [Catholic Bishops' Conference of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Bishops'_Conference_of_the_Philippines "Catholic Bishops' Conference of the Philippines"), and was a member of its permanent council (to which all Filipino Catholic bishops belong).

Title: Venerable Fr. Felix Varela - Our First Pastor
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
**FOR A DISTINGUISHED NATIVE OF THE CARIBBEAN**, it was a rude welcome to America. Fr. Félix Varela, a renowned Cuban philosopher, educator, writer, and statesman, arrived in New York Harbor on December 15, 1823, disembarking from the cargo ship Draper C. Thorndike and stepping into a full-blown blizzard. Unfamiliar with the perils of walking in a northern winter, on his first steps in the country where he would live the next three decades, he slipped and fell on an icy walkway.
It was an unaccustomed low point in the life of the 35-year-old priest. A few weeks earlier, he had been representing Cuba, then a Spanish colony, as a delegate to the nascent legislative assembly at Cádiz, Spain. In a swift turn of events, the deposed Spanish king had been restored to power and ordered the execution of all who had advocated democracy. Facing certain death if he remained in Europe or returned to his beloved Cuba, Varela escaped at night to Gibraltar, where he boarded the _Thorndike,_ bound for New York.
Suddenly an exile, the thin priest in his thin cloak stood up from the icy harborside pavement and found his footing in the streets of a new city. Over the next quarter of a century, he would become a humble but prominent force in the Catholic community there, serving the faithful of New York with a selfless devotion that matched the patriotic fervor he felt for his homeland.
> **_"FATHER VARELA . . . HELPS US TO LIVE OUR FAITH AS A FORCE FOR CHANGE IN SOCIETY. SEEING HIS EXAMPLE, WE CAN OFFER OUR OWN CONTRIBUTION WITH THE SAME ENTHUSIASM THAT HE HAD FOR HELPING THE SOCIETIES OF HIS TIME TO LIVE ACCORDING TO JUSTICE AND TRUTH."_**  
> ARCHBISHOP VINCENZO PAGLIA, POSTULATOR IN VARELA’S CAUSE FOR CANONIZATION

Félix Varela would never again set foot in Cuba, but he also never stopped working on behalf of its people, pointing the way for them toward a freedom that would not come in his lifetime. Two centuries later, he is still revered by Cubans and Cuban-Americans of all political persuasions. The cause for his canonization, initiated in the 1980s, is principally overseen by the Archdiocese of Havana. But it is his life after 1823 – his years as a New York priest – that mark Varela unmistakably as a man of God.
**FÉLIX VARELA Y MORALES WAS BORN**into a military family in Havana, Cuba, in 1788. Orphaned at the age of 3, he was raised by his paternal grandparents in St. Augustine, Florida, where his grandfather was commander of the Spanish garrison. An intelligent, curious child, slight in stature, young Félix took eagerly to his studies in Latin, religion, and history.
When Varela was 14, his grandfather told him it was time to turn from academic pursuits and enroll in military training. The boy politely refused. “I want to be a soldier of Jesus Christ,” he said. When the commander became angry, Félix responded, “I don’t wish to kill men. I want to save their souls.” Though he was not destined to be a warrior, young Varela did not lack for courage.
Instead of a military academy, his grandfather sent Varela to the Seminary of San Carlos in Havana. There the young man was quickly recognized as a rising star. He became a priest, a professor, and by his mid-twenties, one of the colony’s foremost philosophers and thinkers.
As a professor and speaker, Varela showed no fear in exploring and expanding the potentially dangerous ideas of the era he lived in: the abolition of slavery, the overthrow of absolute monarchies and colonial empires. He became known as a speaker who explained ideas so clearly and persuasively that even those who disagreed with him sat up and listened. As a writer, teacher, and delegate to the Spanish Cortes, the priest stood up for what he believed in.

**AFTER HIS LANDING IN AMERICA**, it took Varela more than a year to get his credentials verified to serve as a priest in the Diocese of New York. By February 1825, he had begun serving as a parochial vicar at St. Peter’s Church on Barclay Street in Manhattan. He had learned to speak English, and had begun to settle into his duties: saying Mass, hearing confessions, performing baptisms, visiting the sick. In the evenings, the priest also found time to write and edit _El Habanero_, a magazine for Cuban readers. And the rulers of Spain and Cuba still wanted him dead.
In March 1825, an assassin landed in New York City, dispatched by associates of Francisco Vives, the colonial governor of Cuba. His instructions: to kill Fr. Félix Varela.
The priest received a letter of warning. His friends in the Cuban expatriate community were able to learn the assassin’s identity, but not his whereabouts. They entreated Varela to go into hiding, but he refused. Instead, he went about his business apparently unperturbed. He was not going to let threats turn him from his new mission of helping to build the Catholic Church in America, ministering to the needs of its people.
One day, walking the streets of his parish, the priest encountered the man who had been sent to murder him. In a spirit of compassionate forgiveness, he approached the would-be assassin and counseled him against committing a grave sin. The man listened. Then he returned to Cuba, his mission unfulfilled, while Varela carried on his own with hardly a pause.
**BEFORE THE AMERICAN REVOLUTION**, under British rule, Catholicism was banned in New York. Five decades later, as Varela began his priesthood there, a strong anti-Catholic sentiment still prevailed among many in the Protestant majority. Catholics had to be careful. They could be assaulted in the streets. On one occasion, hundreds of Catholics had to form a human shield around St. Patrick’s Cathedral on Mulberry Street (now known as the Basilica of Old St. Patrick’s Cathedral) to stop a Protestant mob from ransacking and burning it.

There were two Catholic churches in New York City in 1825: St. Patrick’s Cathedral and St. Peter’s Church on Barclay Street. The diocese opened a third, St. Mary’s, in a former Presbyterian church building on Sheriff Street, in 1826; and the following year, Varela, using his own funds and money raised from the community, purchased a fourth: an old Episcopal church in Ann Street called Christ Church. Varela became pastor of a new Catholic parish there. Its population was generally very poor, and most of the money to operate it came from Varela’s supporters in Cuba and New York.
> **_"FATHER VARELA DEDICATED HIS LIFE TO THE SICK, THE POOR, AND THE HELPLESS. HE WAS CALLED ‘THE APOSTLE OF THE IRISH’ FOR HIS WORK WELCOMING IMMIGRANTS AND TENDING TO THEIR NEEDS."_**  
> BISHOP OCTAVIO CISNEROS, VICE POSTULATOR IN VARELA’S CAUSE FOR CANONIZATION
The skills and the passion for justice that Félix Varela had developed in the first 35 years of his life turned out to be just what the Catholic Church in New York needed. His command of the principals of governing served the Church well when parish board members made unruly demands; his problem-solving skills helped keep parishes financially solvent; and his command of language enabled him to build strong community bonds. His talents at oratory captivated congregations during his homilies and, at public forums, unmasked the distortions of demagogues fomenting anti-Catholic sentiment.
Soon he was writing articles in English and co-publishing the _New York Weekly Register and Catholic Diary,_ which was widely read among the immigrant Irish. He wrote an English-language catechism for religious education and opened free Catholic schools for girls and boys next door to Christ Church, where he oversaw instruction and taught many classes himself. The schoolchildren there could hardly have imagined they were being taught by one of the most celebrated professors in the Americas.

opened.information:
Source: https://www.staugustine.com/story/news/local/2011/12/18/father-felix-varelas-cause-sainthood-advances/16187909007/
Title: Father Felix Varela's cause for sainthood advances
Chunks: 0,1,2
Margo C. Pope
Dec. 17, 2011, 11:57 p.m. ET
Father Felix Varela's possible elevation to Venerable - two levels before sainthood in the Roman Catholic Church - is moving forward, says Brother Rodolfo Meoli, the postulator for Varela before the Congregation for the Causes of Saints.
Varela, a 19th-century Cuban priest-patriot, lived here as a youth and worked in St. Augustine's Catholic Church from 1847 to 1852, months before his death in 1853. Varela's push for human rights and independence for Cuba forced him into exile to avoid a death sentence by King Ferdinand in 1823. He spent nearly 30 years as a priest and was Vicar General of the Diocese of New York.
The theologians, whose names are not known to Meoli, were appointed by the Congregation for the Causes of Saints to investigate Varela's life and commitment to the faith. When the promoter for the cause told Meoli on Wednesday that, "Everything is well now," it signaled a new chapter in Varela's cause. They had accepted Meoli's responses in the document - the "Congratio de Causis Sanctorum" of Servant of God Feliz Varela. that is Varela's current rank on the road to sainthood. The next review will be in February by a panel of the church's hierarchy: cardinals and bishops. If they affirm the report, a recommendation will go to Pope Benedict XVI who makes the final decision.
Meoli is cautiously optimistic.
"When the pope will go to Cuba, almost for sure but you can't say with certainty, the pope will bring with him the decree of venerability of Felix Varela. After that, we need to wait for a miracle. And if (a miracle) is proven, then we will arrive at the point of beatification. Nobody knows when that will happen." If there is a second miracle, then canonization will be conferred. There is no timetable for this step either.
"I will be with him," he said, eyes looking upward.
**Postulator plays key role**

As postulator, Meoli is responsible for helping to move Varela's cause forward. It took Meoli almost three years and 147 pages to respond to questions about Varela that the nine theologians posed in 2008. Ironically the major reference to build his responses was a biography about Varela written by Jose Ignacio Rodriquez and published in 1878. Meoli used a copy of the book loaned to him by Bishop Felipe J. Estévez, now head of the Diocese of St. Augustine.
The book, Meoli said, is important because it included information from people in the 19th century who had personal knowledge of Varela's work in Cuba, in the Spanish Cortes in Spain and in the United States.
Meoli was in St. Augustine through Saturday as part of an American tour to acquaint Americans with Varela. Meoli spoke in Jacksonville last week about Varela at St. Paul's Catholic Church. In St. Augustine, he visited Tolomato Cemetery and the Diocesan Archives at St. Joseph Convent. He visited Miami and will be in Philadelphia until Dec. 22.
Meoli was appointed postulator in 2004. He succeeded LaSallian Brother Leone Morelli, the first postulator from 1996 to 2003.
The initial effort on behalf of Varela began in 1985 when Cuban bishops asked the Vatican for permission to pursue Varela's canonization. The first position report on Varela was in 1996 but the process, Meoli said, "went very fast" and "wasn't complete." That preceded Pope John Paul II's visit to Cuba in 1998. During his visit, the pope spoke of Varela's holiness and his commitment to human rights but made no decree.
Meoli, a member of the LaSallian Order, spoke primarily through translators Jahaan Daee and Piotr Skrodzki, although he does speak some English.

In an email to _The Record_, Estévez said, "The canonization of Father Varela is deeply desired by the faithful in the island (Cuba).It is important for us also because Father Varela was deeply connected to St. Augustine where he received his elementary and secondary education and where he lived the last four years of his life and where his tomb stands out at Tolomato cemetery. Brother Meoli has played a significant role in this process providing his expertise to this cause with total generosity.
"We need those exemplary stories to motivate us on the call of holiness. We need to pray for his (Varela's) recognition by the Church for our own good."
*
Felix Varela, 1788-1853, came to St. Augustine in 1791 with his grandparents, Lt. Col. Bartolme and Rita Morales, at the age of 3. His parents had died. His grandfather was the commanding officer of the Third Battalion of Cuba, assigned to St. Augustine. His first home was likely St. Francis Barracks, now the state headquarters of the Florida National Guard.
- Susan Parker, Ph.D., executive director of the St. Augustine Historical Society.
*
Varela first returned to St. Augustine in 1844 for health reasons and then for good in 1846. His work at the St. Augustine Catholic Church included saying Mass, presiding at baptisms, weddings and funerals and operating a school for boys. His name appears in church records from 1847 to 1852. In 1892, Cuban patriot Jose Marti visited Varela's burial chapel in Tolomato Cemetery and called Varela, the "Cuban saint."
- Source: Cathedral records and the St. Augustine Historical Society

Title: Mother Juana de la Cruz, 1481–1534: Visionary Sermons
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
The Marian Apocalyptic of a Visionary Preacher: The Conorte of Juana de la Cruz, 1481–1534
The End of the World in Medieval Thought and Spirituality, 2019
Mother Juana de la Cruz (1481-1534), abbess of a Clarisan convent outside Toledo, Spain, preached publically for thirteen years, putatively channeling Jesus’ voice through her raptured body. This chapter argues that Juana’s blend of apocalyptic genres was a forerunner of the “Marian apocalyptic” described by E. Ann Matter for the 20th century. This genre of private Marian apparitions designated the seer, Juana, as authoritative, yet disseminated apocalyptic material through publically preached visions of the otherworld. Not only did these visions interweave interpretations of apocalyptic symbols with discussions of the fate of individual souls, but Mary herself was presented as an active agent in the otherworld, not simply interceding with Jesus but engaging the devil in battle. I argue that Mary as apocalyptic figure rather than apparitional message-bearer would have resonated strongly with Juana’s Iberian audience, as not only had Mary long been a focal point of devotion during reconquest on the peninsula, but Castilian leaders attempting at establishing an empire in the New World frequently justified their endeavors through apocalyptic rhetoric.
Towards a Critical Edition of the Libro del Conorte of the Abbess Juana de la Cruz (1481-1534)
Observant Reforms and Cultural Production in Europe, B. Roest and P. Delcorno (eds.), 2023

This article constitutes a first effort to organize the materials, reflections and unresolved questions that have emerged from my recent years of study of Juana de la Cruz and the Conorte. If all goes according to plan, this will culminate in both the first critical edition of the text and a monograph on the transcription and collection of her sermons. I would like to offer some preliminary reflections on the material evidence of this case in order to highlight specifically the need for a re-evaluation of the codices containing the Conorte and also of the discourse containing the actual words uttered by Juana. Margo C. Pope
Dec. 17, 2011, 11:57 p.m. ET
Father Felix Varela's possible elevation to Venerable - two levels before sainthood in the Roman Catholic Church - is moving forward, says Brother Rodolfo Meoli, the postulator for Varela before the Congregation for the Causes of Saints.
Varela, a 19th-century Cuban priest-patriot, lived here as a youth and worked in St. Augustine's Catholic Church from 1847 to 1852, months before his death in 1853. Varela's push for human rights and independence for Cuba forced him into exile to avoid a death sentence by King Ferdinand in 1823. He spent nearly 30 years as a priest and was Vicar General of the Diocese of New York.
The theologians, whose names are not known to Meoli, were appointed by the Congregation for the Causes of Saints to investigate Varela's life and commitment to the faith. When the promoter for the cause told Meoli on Wednesday that, "Everything is well now," it signaled a new chapter in Varela's cause. They had accepted Meoli's responses in the document - the "Congratio de Causis Sanctorum" of Servant of God Feliz Varela. that is Varela's current rank on the road to sainthood. The next review will be in February by a panel of the church's hierarchy: cardinals and bishops. If they affirm the report, a recommendation will go to Pope Benedict XVI who makes the final decision.
Meoli is cautiously optimistic.
"When the pope will go to Cuba, almost for sure but you can't say with certainty, the pope will bring with him the decree of venerability of Felix Varela. After that, we need to wait for a miracle. And if (a miracle) is proven, then we will arrive at the point of beatification. Nobody knows when that will happen." If there is a second miracle, then canonization will be conferred. There is no timetable for this step either.
"I will be with him," he said, eyes looking upward.
**Postulator plays key role**
texts.1:
As postulator, Meoli is responsible for helping to move Varela's cause forward. It took Meoli almost three years and 147 pages to respond to questions about Varela that the nine theologians posed in 2008. Ironically the major reference to build his responses was a biography about Varela written by Jose Ignacio Rodriquez and published in 1878. Meoli used a copy of the book loaned to him by Bishop Felipe J. Estévez, now head of the Diocese of St. Augustine.
The book, Meoli said, is important because it included information from people in the 19th century who had personal knowledge of Varela's work in Cuba, in the Spanish Cortes in Spain and in the United States.
Meoli was in St. Augustine through Saturday as part of an American tour to acquaint Americans with Varela. Meoli spoke in Jacksonville last week about Varela at St. Paul's Catholic Church. In St. Augustine, he visited Tolomato Cemetery and the Diocesan Archives at St. Joseph Convent. He visited Miami and will be in Philadelphia until Dec. 22.
Meoli was appointed postulator in 2004. He succeeded LaSallian Brother Leone Morelli, the first postulator from 1996 to 2003.
The initial effort on behalf of Varela began in 1985 when Cuban bishops asked the Vatican for permission to pursue Varela's canonization. The first position report on Varela was in 1996 but the process, Meoli said, "went very fast" and "wasn't complete." That preceded Pope John Paul II's visit to Cuba in 1998. During his visit, the pope spoke of Varela's holiness and his commitment to human rights but made no decree.
Meoli, a member of the LaSallian Order, spoke primarily through translators Jahaan Daee and Piotr Skrodzki, although he does speak some English.
texts.2:
In an email to _The Record_, Estévez said, "The canonization of Father Varela is deeply desired by the faithful in the island (Cuba).It is important for us also because Father Varela was deeply connected to St. Augustine where he received his elementary and secondary education and where he lived the last four years of his life and where his tomb stands out at Tolomato cemetery. Brother Meoli has played a significant role in this process providing his expertise to this cause with total generosity.
"We need those exemplary stories to motivate us on the call of holiness. We need to pray for his (Varela's) recognition by the Church for our own good."
*
Felix Varela, 1788-1853, came to St. Augustine in 1791 with his grandparents, Lt. Col. Bartolme and Rita Morales, at the age of 3. His parents had died. His grandfather was the commanding officer of the Third Battalion of Cuba, assigned to St. Augustine. His first home was likely St. Francis Barracks, now the state headquarters of the Florida National Guard.
- Susan Parker, Ph.D., executive director of the St. Augustine Historical Society.
*
Varela first returned to St. Augustine in 1844 for health reasons and then for good in 1846. His work at the St. Augustine Catholic Church included saying Mass, presiding at baptisms, weddings and funerals and operating a school for boys. His name appears in church records from 1847 to 1852. In 1892, Cuban patriot Jose Marti visited Varela's burial chapel in Tolomato Cemetery and called Varela, the "Cuban saint."
- Source: Cathedral records and the St. Augustine Historical Society

The book, Meoli said, is important because it included information from people in the 19th century who had personal knowledge of Varela's work in Cuba, in the Spanish Cortes in Spain and in the United States.
Meoli was in St. Augustine through Saturday as part of an American tour to acquaint Americans with Varela. Meoli spoke in Jacksonville last week about Varela at St. Paul's Catholic Church. In St. Augustine, he visited Tolomato Cemetery and the Diocesan Archives at St. Joseph Convent. He visited Miami and will be in Philadelphia until Dec. 22.
Meoli was appointed postulator in 2004. He succeeded LaSallian Brother Leone Morelli, the first postulator from 1996 to 2003.
The initial effort on behalf of Varela began in 1985 when Cuban bishops asked the Vatican for permission to pursue Varela's canonization. The first position report on Varela was in 1996 but the process, Meoli said, "went very fast" and "wasn't complete." That preceded Pope John Paul II's visit to Cuba in 1998. During his visit, the pope spoke of Varela's holiness and his commitment to human rights but made no decree.
Meoli, a member of the LaSallian Order, spoke primarily through translators Jahaan Daee and Piotr Skrodzki, although he does speak some English.

In an email to _The Record_, Estévez said, "The canonization of Father Varela is deeply desired by the faithful in the island (Cuba).It is important for us also because Father Varela was deeply connected to St. Augustine where he received his elementary and secondary education and where he lived the last four years of his life and where his tomb stands out at Tolomato cemetery. Brother Meoli has played a significant role in this process providing his expertise to this cause with total generosity.
"We need those exemplary stories to motivate us on the call of holiness. We need to pray for his (Varela's) recognition by the Church for our own good."
*
Felix Varela, 1788-1853, came to St. Augustine in 1791 with his grandparents, Lt. Col. Bartolme and Rita Morales, at the age of 3. His parents had died. His grandfather was the commanding officer of the Third Battalion of Cuba, assigned to St. Augustine. His first home was likely St. Francis Barracks, now the state headquarters of the Florida National Guard.
- Susan Parker, Ph.D., executive director of the St. Augustine Historical Society.
*
Varela first returned to St. Augustine in 1844 for health reasons and then for good in 1846. His work at the St. Augustine Catholic Church included saying Mass, presiding at baptisms, weddings and funerals and operating a school for boys. His name appears in church records from 1847 to 1852. In 1892, Cuban patriot Jose Marti visited Varela's burial chapel in Tolomato Cemetery and called Varela, the "Cuban saint."
- Source: Cathedral records and the St. Augustine Historical Society

Source: https://www.academia.edu/26070752/Mother_Juana_de_la_Cruz_1481_1534_Visionary_Sermons
Title: Mother Juana de la Cruz, 1481–1534: Visionary Sermons
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
The Marian Apocalyptic of a Visionary Preacher: The Conorte of Juana de la Cruz, 1481–1534
The End of the World in Medieval Thought and Spirituality, 2019
Mother Juana de la Cruz (1481-1534), abbess of a Clarisan convent outside Toledo, Spain, preached publically for thirteen years, putatively channeling Jesus’ voice through her raptured body. This chapter argues that Juana’s blend of apocalyptic genres was a forerunner of the “Marian apocalyptic” described by E. Ann Matter for the 20th century. This genre of private Marian apparitions designated the seer, Juana, as authoritative, yet disseminated apocalyptic material through publically preached visions of the otherworld. Not only did these visions interweave interpretations of apocalyptic symbols with discussions of the fate of individual souls, but Mary herself was presented as an active agent in the otherworld, not simply interceding with Jesus but engaging the devil in battle. I argue that Mary as apocalyptic figure rather than apparitional message-bearer would have resonated strongly with Juana’s Iberian audience, as not only had Mary long been a focal point of devotion during reconquest on the peninsula, but Castilian leaders attempting at establishing an empire in the New World frequently justified their endeavors through apocalyptic rhetoric.
Towards a Critical Edition of the Libro del Conorte of the Abbess Juana de la Cruz (1481-1534)
Observant Reforms and Cultural Production in Europe, B. Roest and P. Delcorno (eds.), 2023

This article constitutes a first effort to organize the materials, reflections and unresolved questions that have emerged from my recent years of study of Juana de la Cruz and the Conorte. If all goes according to plan, this will culminate in both the first critical edition of the text and a monograph on the transcription and collection of her sermons. I would like to offer some preliminary reflections on the material evidence of this case in order to highlight specifically the need for a re-evaluation of the codices containing the Conorte and also of the discourse containing the actual words uttered by Juana. In the first part of the paper therefore, I present the two different manuscripts that include Juana’s sermons and revisit their implications in the history of Juana’s canonization process in order to address certain codicological, philological and ideological issues that need to be urgently re-considered before a hermeneutic reading of the text can take place. In the second part, I try to identify what we understand by the Conorte or, in other words,what we know and do not know about its collective writing, compilation, and use by the community of the Convent of Santa María de la Cruz.
OPEN ACCESS! The Visionary Preaching of Juana de la Cruz (1481-1534). Ritual, Revelation, and Collective Writing
2025
Step into the world of 16th-century Castile, where a devout community of Franciscan women preserved the public preaching of their visionary abbess, Juana de la Cruz (1481-1534), through writing. This groundbreaking book uncovers how her sermons were recorded, explores the materiality of the surviving codices, and reveals their role in the controversial censorship and blocking of Juana’s canonization. Tracing the rich tradition of the liturgical vision (12th-16th centuries), it delves into female literacy and the creation of collective knowledge in female religious houses around Europe. Featuring rare insights and fresh evaluations of historical texts, this volume illuminates the intersection of female prophetic preaching, community, and the written word at the end of the Middle Ages.
Franciscan Preaching at the Turn of the Sixteenth Century: Contextualizing Jean Vitrier
From Learning to Love. Essays in Honour of Joseph W. Goering, 2017

Following Etienne Gilson's classic essay "Michel Menot et la technique da serman medievale, "2 and the forays of Harry Caplan in the medieval art ofpreaching, 3 the form and structure of medieval scholastic preaching has drawn the attention of a large number of medievalists. This has opened up a massive amount of source material to specialist scrutiny, and has done much to enlighten us about the ways in which doctrinal instruction as well as the propagation of specific devotions took place. It also has had a somewhat cumbersome side effect, namely, the renewed emphasis on the distance between later medieval scholastic preaching, epitomized by the so-called sermo modernus, and its alleged humanist and Protestant successors: humanist oratory and the evangelical homily, variations of which combined patrisdc models with new rhetorical guidelines.
Preaching Christ in a Transcultural Society: The Homiliary of Luculentius from Early Medieval Catalonia (ca. 900)
In the twenty-first century, the chance to discover, study and edit a quasi-unknown and disregarded Latin text from the Early Medieval Ages is remarkably rare. The Homiliary of Luculentius offers us this exceptional opportunity. All current indicators favour our hypothesis that this considerable source, known only from selected parts, is a rarity in the proper sense: it appears to be the earliest autochthonous monument of Latin literature of the so-called Spanish March, the north-eastern part of the Iberian Peninsula dominated by the Carolingians and their culture. Our new research project aims at the full edition of this work, the identification of its sources and the religious, social and political contextualisation of the probably monastic author and his network. The exploration of this work will fundamentally change our vision of Carolingian culture in a still-underrated periphery of Charlemagne’s Empire.
Valencia's Miraculous Prophet: The Inquisition Dossier of Catalina Muñoz (1588)
postmedieval: a journal of medieval cultural studies, 2019

Preserved in the archives of the National Historic Archive in Madrid, the life story of Catalina Muñ oz uncovers the ways in which she, as a triply marginalized subject-black, woman, and slave-obtained power and social clout by capitalizing on the fame she acquired because of her role as spiritual advisor and healer to the Valencian religious community of Sanct Martín Church. This essay positions Catalina as an astute agent and spiritual advisor who navigated with savvy the intricacies of Valencia's sixteenth-century religious elite. In doing so, the article aims to reassign and parse Catalina's agency as a prophet. It is through the caveat of prophecy where Catalina obtains her power and position by capitalizing on the fame-often referred to as 'escá ndolo' ['scandal']-she acquired as a spiritual advisor and healer to the Valencian religious communities. (2019) 10, 36-49.

Lord Jesus, who took the form of a servant and did not grasp at Your own divine privileges — thank You for the quiet, foundational ministry of Bishop Concordio Sarte during his years as Auxiliary Bishop of Sorsogon, for his patience, his willingness to step into a fractured house, and his steady endurance under the shadow of institutional breaking. Train us by Your appeared Grace to value the hidden seasons of supportive service. Deliver us from the toxic need for immediate control, public recognition, or quick resolutions when a crisis surrounds us. Give us the spiritual maturity to maintain the household of faith through our quiet presence, our unglamorous labor, and our relentless charity. May we anchor our identity so deeply in Your finished work that we are content to be hidden instruments, keeping the peace until Your hour of restoration comes.
Amen.
DAY 42 — THE BRIDGE BUILDER: BISHOP SARTE'S EMERGENCY MINISTRY ▼
a.. BIBLICAL QUOTE
"Blessed are the peacemakers,
for they shall be called sons of God."
(Matthew 5:9)
b.. HISTORY
When the Vatican determined that the Diocese of Sorsogon required direct intervention, it did not immediately appoint a new Bishop. What was needed first was a peacemaker — someone who could enter the war zone of a broken Diocese, lift the canonical penalties that had fractured the presbyterium, begin the work of genuine reconciliation, and prepare the ground on which a new Bishop could eventually build. Pope John Paul II appointed Bishop Concordio Maria Sarte as Apostolic Administrator Sede Vacante of the Diocese of Sorsogon. His mission was precisely defined and extraordinarily demanding: restore basic order, lift the canonical penalties on the traumatized priests, and find a way to reopen the seminary and the institutional structures of the Diocese. He was not building a new Diocese. He was creating the conditions in which building would eventually become possible.

He conducted this ministry in the shadow of Martial Law — navigating not only the canonical complexity of a fractured presbyterium but the political complexity of an authoritarian regime that viewed organized community gatherings with suspicion. The sheer stress of this ministry took an immense physical and emotional toll on Bishop Sarte. He completed his bridge-building work and was transferred to become the Bishop of Legazpi in August 1980, his Apostolic Administrator role ending by December 1980 — not leaving behind a fully healed Diocese, but at least one no longer in immediate danger of total collapse, with the canonical penalties lifted, the worst of the acute crisis resolved, and the ground prepared for the rebuilder who was coming.
c.. TETELESTAI
The ministry of the peacemaker illuminates a dimension of the finished work that dramatic moments of founding and reform cannot fully reveal: Tetelestai is the ground of the costly reconciliation that no human authority can manufacture. The Cross was the supreme act of reconciliation — not the superficial reconciliation of a conflict resolved by compromise, but the deep, costly, death-requiring reconciliation of a breach so fundamental that only the giving of the Son of God could bridge it. Every act of genuine reconciliation in the particular Church participates in this finished work — is sustained by it, draws its possibility from it, and reflects in its own specific and limited way the logic of the One who crossed the infinite distance between holiness and sin to bridge what nothing else could bridge.
The beatitude of Matthew 5:9 — blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God — is a beatitude specifically about the Cross. Those who participate in His peacemaking — who enter the broken relationships and fractured communities that others prefer to avoid — are called His sons and daughters because they are doing what He did, in the power of what He accomplished.
Bishop Sarte stepping into the breach of the broken Diocese was a local, canonical, historically specific participation in the reconciling movement of the Cross — the peacemaker going where the peace was most needed, at personal cost, into the most acute institutional conflict the Diocese had ever experienced.
d.. GRACE APPEARED

The ministry of Bishop Sarte was one of the most demanding expressions of the self-controlled, upright, and godly life that Titus 2:12 describes — conducted in the most difficult possible circumstances, without the support of a settled institutional structure, without visible fruit, and without the prospect of the historical recognition that more celebrated ministries receive. Self-controlled: the discipline of entering acute institutional conflict without being drawn into its partisanship. Upright: the honest, transparent exercise of the Apostolic Administrator's authority — lifting canonical penalties that had been unjustly imposed, restoring priests to the exercise of their ministry. Godly: the continuous orientation of the entire ministry toward the God whose finished work was the foundation of the reconciliation being attempted.
The appeared Grace trained Bishop Sarte through this specific, costly, brief, and largely invisible ministry in a way that no more celebrated role could have produced. The formation of the peacemaker is the formation of the one who enters the breach — and the breach of the Diocese of Sorsogon in the late 1970s was one of the most demanding breaches any bishop in the Philippine Church had ever been asked to enter.
e.. TODAY'S ACTION
Is there a fractured relationship, a broken community, a conflict in your parish or your family or your small community that needs a bridge builder — someone willing to enter the breach at personal cost, without the guarantee of historical recognition, for the sake of the reconciliation that the finished work demands? Ask the appeared Grace today whether you are being called to that role. And if you know someone currently serving as a bridge builder in a difficult situation — a priest navigating a parish conflict, a lay leader mediating a community division, a family member holding fractured relationships together at personal cost — honor them today. The peacemakers are the sons and daughters of God.
f.. PRAYER
Lord Jesus, supreme Peacemaker whose finished work is the foundation of all genuine reconciliation — thank You for Bishop Concordio Sarte, who entered the breach of the Diocese of Sorsogon at immense personal cost to hold Your house together during its darkest storm. Grant us the same self-controlled, upright, and godly grace to step into the fractured spaces of our own lives. Teach us to become true bridge builders, content to labor in the background, drawing our strength solely from the complete reconciliation You secured on Calvary. Amen.

DIOCESE OF SORSOGON ✦ 75TH DIAMOND JUBILEE
PILGRIMS OF HOPE
DAY 43 — THE HISTORIC FIRST DIOCESAN PASTORAL ASSEMBLY ▼
A.. BIBLICAL QUOTE
"Let every person
be quick to hear,
slow to speak."
(James 1:19)
B.. HISTORY
When Bishop Jesus Y. Varela was named third Bishop of Sorsogon on November 27, 1980 and installed on December 12, 1980, he inherited a Diocese in crisis. The years before his arrival had seen a severe breakdown between the Bishop and his priests — canonical penalties, a closed seminary, and displaced clergy sheltered by lay families. The Diocese was wounded, divided, and financially depleted. Rather than imposing his own plan immediately, Bishop Varela did something unexpected: he partnered with the Southeast Asia Interdisciplinary Development Institute (SAIDI) for a collaborative process and called everyone together for the first General Assembly. Throughout 1981, while still experiencing the offshoot of Martial Law — lifted in January for Pope John Paul II's coming in February — the Diocese underwent intense, ground-level diagnostic workshops, data gathering, and pastoral assemblies.
This historic gathering of deep, structured listening healed local wounds and successfully paved the way for the planning, alignment, and consultation that gave birth to the First Diocesan Pastoral Plan (DPP-I). That gathering — the first Diocesan Pastoral Assembly — became the moment the Diocese of Sorsogon chose a new way of being Church.
C.. TETELESTAI
The finished work of the Cross does not only cancel the debt of personal sin. It cancels the debt of division — the broken trust, the wounded relationships, the fractured community that human failure produces. When Jesus declared Tetelestai, He was announcing that the wall between God and humanity had fallen — and that the same power could bring down the walls between people.
The first Pastoral Assembly was Tetelestai made institutional — the Diocese choosing, because of the finished work, to build on listening rather than on authority alone.

❖ Which of these three forms of the finished work — the long view, the open hand, or the intimate community — does your family, small community, or chapel community most need to receive more deeply right now? Share briefly and let the sharing become a communal prayer for that specific reception.
Movement 2 — Grace Has Appeared: The Training of the Pruning Season
The appeared Grace conducted a specific and demanding training of the Diocese of Sorsogon in the Set 7 era: the training toward the patient, the generous, and the relationally steady. Patient — through the consolidating tenure of Bishop Arcilla, forming the Diocese in the self-controlled, upright, and godly life of the community that trusts the appeared Grace's pace. Generous — through the separation of Masbate, forming the Diocese in the kenotic open-handedness of a community that can release what it has been given when the fullness of time calls it to release it. Relationally steady — through the Bishop Sarte interim, training the local Church to maintain the household of faith during a season of severe structural collapse, proving that the life of the gospel is sustained from the ground up by quiet peacemaking, shared suffering, and basic pastoral care even when the primary administrative engines have ground to a halt.
Each of these three training movements required a specific renunciation: the patience required the renunciation of restless novelty; the generosity required the renunciation of possessiveness; the relational steadiness required the renunciation of institutional panic that measures the survival of a particular Church by the visibility of its top-down structures rather than by the quiet, Christ-centered endurance of its people in the breach.
❖ Which of these three renunciations — of restless novelty, of possessiveness, or of institutional panic — is the appeared Grace most specifically calling your community to make in this season? Name it honestly. And name one concrete expression of that renunciation that your community could make this month.
Movement 3 — Pilgrims of Hope: The Family as the Basic Unit of the Pilgrimage

The Pilgrim of Hope does not walk the pilgrimage alone. The most basic unit of the communal journey is your small community — the community of the finished work in its most local, most intimate, most practically engaged form. Every small community that gathers in a barangay chapel before dawn is walking the same pilgrimage as the Bishop in his Cathedral — toward the same blessed hope, sustained by the same finished work, trained by the same appeared Grace, contributing its specific portion of the communal witness that the Diocese offers to the watching world.
The Pilgrims of Hope who walk in small communities are not lesser pilgrims than those who walk in the more visible institutional structures of the Diocese. They are the foundational pilgrims — the ones whose faithful, locally rooted, relational, Word-and-Eucharist-centered walking forms the base of the particular Church's pilgrimage. The lay families who opened their homes during the crisis years were exactly these foundational pilgrims — sustaining the Diocese from the ground up when its top-down structures had collapsed. Without them, the Diocese's pilgrimage would be an institutional procession without a people. With them, it is the whole People of God walking together toward the blessed hope.
❖ What specific step can your small community or chapel community take this month to deepen its participation in the pilgrimage — to be more fully the Acts 2:42 community devoted to the apostles' teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and the prayers? Name it. Assign it. Date it.
Part Three — Respond
The facilitator invites the group to make one concrete communal commitment for the coming month, using the following framework:
Our Masbate — What is the thing your community has been holding that the appeared Grace may be calling you to release — generously, openly, without grasping — so that it can develop its own independent fruitfulness? A ministry, a responsibility, a person being formed for a larger role, a resource that belongs more fully to another community's mission? Name it. Pray over it. Begin the process of generous release this month.
Our Bishop Sarte Interim — What is the transitional season your community is currently navigating — the period of institutional uncertainty that requires faithful bridging rather than anxious grasping or passive waiting? Name it. Identify what faithful stewardship of this specific transitional moment looks like. Commit to one act of active, forward-leaning, mission-sustaining faithfulness in the transition.

Our Small Community — What is the one specific good work that your family, small community, or chapel community will commit to this month as its participation in the zealous good works of Titus 2:14 — specific, concrete, neighborhood-scaled, relationally grounded? Name the need. Name the response. Name the people responsible. Set the date.
Closing Prayer
Lord Jesus, True Vine who prunes, Good Shepherd who does not leave us orphaned, Bread of Life who nourishes the most intimate gathering of neighbors around Your finished work — we receive today the formation of the pruning season: the patience of the consolidator, the generosity of the open hand, the locally specific faithfulness of the small community. Restore in us the patient trust that does not impose its own urgency on Your pace. Renew in us the kenotic generosity that releases what You are calling us to release without grasping. Deepen in us the locally specific engagement with the people and the place You have specifically entrusted to our community's care. We are Pilgrims of Hope, walking the pilgrimage in small communities and Cathedral congregations alike, all of us sustained by the same finished work, all of us trained by the same appeared Grace, all of us oriented toward the same blessed hope of Your return. Keep us faithful, Lord — patient, generous, and locally specific — all the way to the glory that is coming.
Amen.
(Close with a few minutes of silence. Then send the group forth.)
Note for facilitators: The three commitments — Our Masbate, Our Bishop Sarte Interim, Our Small Community — address three distinct aspects of the Set 7 era's formation. A community holding too tightly to something will find the first most urgent. A community in transition will find the second most immediately relevant. A community whose small community life has grown routine or thin will find the third most challenging. Use what serves your specific group. The goal remains one concrete communal commitment, named, assigned, and dated.
Monthly Workshop Study — Set 8
Structural Renewal and Communion
For Small Communities, Chapel Groups, and Parish Organizations | 45–60 min (facilitator adds discussion time)
Opening Prayer

Lord Jesus, You built Your Church not on a throne but on a Cross — the servant leadership of the One who gave everything so that everyone could belong. As we gather today, open our ears to hear what the appeared Grace is saying to our community through the Diocese of Sorsogon's journey of structural renewal and communal listening. We are Pilgrims of Hope — teach us to walk together.
Amen.
Part One — Remember
Read aloud slowly. Invite the group to listen not as students receiving information but as pilgrims receiving their own story.
When Bishop Jesus Varela arrived in Sorsogon in 1980, he inherited a Diocese wounded by crisis — a fractured presbyterium, a closed seminary, and a community that had nearly collapsed under the weight of unaccountable leadership. Rather than rebuilding the same structure that had failed, he chose a radically different foundation: he listened first. Partnering with the Southeast Asia Interdisciplinary Development Institute (SAIDI), the Diocese underwent an entire year of structured communal consultation in 1981. From that listening stance, the first Diocesan Pastoral Plan was born — launched in 1982 with the vision: "Banwaan na may pagtubod, nabubuhay sa pagkamoot, sosog sa marhay na bareta, nagsisimbag sa paglingkod, sa pangangaipo kan panahon, naghihingoha sa paglaom sa pag-abot kan kahadean nin Diyos."
DPP-I organized the Diocese and the parishes into servant structures down to the small neighborhood groupings of families. It established the Parish Pastoral Council with the ME-WESTY framework — six pillars of mission, each with its own lay commission: Media for Evangelization, Worship, Education, Service, Temporalities, and Youth. It commissioned Catechists and Lay Ministers to carry the Word of God and the Eucharist into the chapel communities. And it deepened parish communion through shared formation programs and communal discernment that made all parishes genuinely one body.
